prompt:
以下はある英語ニュースpodcast記事のFull Story・Point One・Point Twoです。
Point One・Point Twoそれぞれについて、以下6項目を判定してください
(それぞれPASS/FAIL)。

- qa_not_caveat_only: このPointが、研究上の限界・一般化上の注意・免責事項
  だけで構成されていない場合PASS(それらに加えて実質的な新しい内容がある
  場合もPASS。留保だけでPoint枠全体が終わっている場合はFAIL)
- qa_not_full_story_paraphrase: Full Storyの要約・言い換えに留まっていない
  場合PASS(Full Storyの中心的なlogic・結論を語彙だけ変えて繰り返している
  場合はFAIL)
- qa_not_other_point_paraphrase: もう一方のPointの要約・言い換えになって
  いない場合PASS
- qa_explains_why_it_matters: 「だから何なのか」を具体的に説明できている
  場合PASS(聞き手にとっての具体的な意味・示唆がある場合)
- qa_specific_not_generic: この記事のLedger固有の内容に基づいており、他の
  どんな記事にもほぼそのまま流用できる一般論になっていない場合PASS
- qa_adds_new_value: 新しい理解・解釈・意外性・具体的示唆のいずれかを
  実際に加えている場合PASS(Full Storyだけを聞いた場合と比べて、聞き手の
  理解が実際に深まっている場合)

reasoningには、判定理由を1〜2文の日本語で書いてください(特にFAILの場合は
具体的な理由を明記してください)。

【Full Story】
Something new has entered the public record about weapons in space. But the change is narrower than many headlines may suggest.

On September 14, 2026, U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said the United States was deploying space-control weapons in orbit. He said they were meant to protect the joint military force from hostile actions.

The next day, an official U.S. Space Force report called this the first public acknowledgment that the Space Force had placed weapons in orbit.

But the report did not name the system, explain its exact attack method, or identify any target.

That matters because earlier anti-satellite tests were different. Russia in 2021, China in 2007, and India in 2019 used missiles launched from Earth to destroy satellites. Those tests showed that a country could attack a satellite from the ground. They did not show that an attack weapon had been stationed in orbit.

In 2024, the U.S. Defense Department also said Russia had placed a satellite in the same orbit as a U.S. government satellite. It judged that the satellite could possibly attack other low-orbit satellites. But no attack was confirmed.

Other U.S. assessments describe Russian and Chinese counterspace abilities as developing or possible. That is not the same as confirming a weapon already deployed in orbit.

Existing rules add another important line. The Outer Space Treaty bans nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in orbit. It also bans military bases and weapons tests on the Moon and other celestial bodies. But it does not completely ban every weapon in space.

UN votes in 2024 and 2025 showed that space arms remain an international issue. They did not create a new, broad treaty banning all space weapons.

【Point One】
For this story, “deploying weapons to space” should mean the newly acknowledged weapons placed in orbit. Russia’s 2021, China’s 2007, and India’s 2019 tests used missiles launched from Earth to destroy satellites. Russia’s 2024 satellite and other abilities judged possible or still developing do not confirm a weapon stationed in orbit. The exact U.S. system remains undisclosed.

【Point Two】
Counterspace is a wider map. The U.S. Space Force uses the term for actions in orbit, through communication links, and on the ground. In 2022, a cyberattack on Viasat’s KA-SAT network caused service problems without destroying the satellite. In 2026, four Russian military satellites moved close to a radar satellite, but no attack was confirmed. HBTSS tracking satellites, GPS, warning, and resilience systems are protective missions, not proof of orbital attack weapons.

point_one.reasoning: 地上発射型の衛星攻撃、ロシア衛星の可能性、米国の軌道上兵器の非公開というFull Storyの中心的な区別をほぼそのまま繰り返している。用語の整理はあるが、それによって何が変わるのかという具体的な示唆や新情報は加えていない。

point_two.reasoning: Counterspaceを軌道上・通信経路・地上での活動を含む広い概念として整理し、Viasatのサイバー攻撃、衛星の接近、HBTSSやGPSなど具体例を追加している。これにより、衛星を破壊する攻撃と妨害・接近・防御的任務を区別でき、Full Storyだけより理解が深まる。
